analogy.p: Imagine a line of cars, each 5 m long bumper to bumper, driving past you. If 4 cars pass each second, then the line is moving at 4 × 5 = 20 m/s. The cars per second is the frequency, the length of each car is the wavelength, and the speed of the line is the wave speed. It breaks down because cars are separate objects that really move forwards, whereas in a wave the medium only vibrates and just the pattern travels.
analogy.t: Cars passing a fixed point on a road

bullets: **Amplitude**: the **maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position**. Unit: metre (or whatever length unit the graph uses).
**Wavelength (λ)**: the **distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave**. Unit: metres (m).
**Frequency (f)**: the **number of waves passing a point each second**. Unit: hertz (Hz).
**Period (T)**: the **time taken for one complete wave to pass a point**. Unit: seconds (s).
**Wave speed (v)**: the **speed at which energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium**. Unit: metres per second (m/s).
Amplitude is about **how big**, wavelength is about **how long in space**, period is about **how long in time**.
core.h: The four quantities that describe a wave
core.p: Every wave, transverse or longitudinal, is described by four measurable quantities: **amplitude**, **wavelength**, **frequency** and **period**. Together with the **wave speed** they let you predict how a wave will behave. You must know each definition in the board wording and be able to read the values from a diagram or graph.

bullets: Crest to trough height = 2 × amplitude.
On a displacement-distance graph, amplitude is the maximum height above the horizontal axis.
Bigger amplitude = more energy carried by the wave (for sound: louder; for light: brighter).
Amplitude does **not** affect the wave speed or the pitch (frequency) of a sound.
As a wave spreads out or is absorbed its amplitude decreases (the wave gets weaker).
Amplitude has the unit of the displacement being measured (m, cm, mm).
core.p: Amplitude tells you how far the wave displaces particles from their rest position, so it is linked to the **energy** the wave carries. It is always measured from the **undisturbed (middle) line** up to a crest or down to a trough, never from crest to trough. A larger amplitude means a louder sound, a brighter light or a taller water wave, but it does not change the speed of the wave or its frequency.

bullets: Measure from crest to crest (or trough to trough): **not** crest to trough (that is λ/2).
For accuracy, measure over several waves and divide: e.g. 5 wavelengths = 1.0 m, so λ = 0.20 m.
Read wavelength from a **displacement-distance graph** (horizontal axis is distance).
Typical values: sound in air 0.017 m to 17 m; visible light about 4 × 10^-7 m to 7 × 10^-7 m; radio waves from centimetres to kilometres.
Convert units before calculating: 1 cm = 0.01 m, 1 mm = 0.001 m, 1 nm = 10^-9 m.
If the frequency stays the same but the speed falls, the wavelength becomes shorter (see v = f λ).
core.p: Wavelength is a distance **in space**: the length of one complete wave. It can be measured between any two equivalent points: crest to crest, trough to trough, or the same point on two adjacent waves. For a longitudinal wave it is the distance between the centres of two adjacent compressions (or rarefactions). It is represented by the Greek letter **lambda (λ)** and measured in metres.

bullets: T = 1 ÷ f (period in s, frequency in Hz). f = 1 ÷ T.
Example: f = 50 Hz means T = 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02 s.
Example: a wave with T = 0.004 s has f = 1 ÷ 0.004 = 250 Hz.
Frequency is the same as the number of **vibrations of the source per second**: a speaker cone vibrating 440 times a second makes a note of 440 Hz.
Larger frequency = shorter period; higher pitch for sound; for light, a different colour or type of EM wave.
Common unit prefixes: 1 kHz = 1000 Hz = 10^3 Hz, 1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz = 10^6 Hz, 1 GHz = 10^9 Hz.
Counting method: frequency = number of waves passing ÷ time taken. 12 waves in 6 s gives 2 Hz.
core.p: **Frequency** is how many complete waves pass a fixed point every second, measured in **hertz (Hz)** where 1 Hz is one wave per second. The **period** is the time taken for one complete wave, so the two are reciprocals of each other: **period = 1 ÷ frequency**, in symbols **T = 1/f**, and also **f = 1/T**. The frequency of a wave is set by the **source** and does not change when the wave moves from one medium to another.

bullets: **v = f λ**: v in m/s, f in Hz, λ in m. You must **recall** this equation (it is not given on the AQA equation sheet).
Rearrangements: **f = v ÷ λ** and **λ = v ÷ f**.
Formula triangle: put v on top and f and λ side by side below; cover the one you want.
Because v = fλ, if the speed is fixed then f and λ are **inversely proportional**: doubling the frequency halves the wavelength.
If the wavelength is fixed, speed is **directly proportional** to frequency.
Show your working: write the equation, substitute with units, calculate, then state the unit.
The wave speed is **not** the speed of the vibrating particles: particles move back and forth about a fixed point while the wave pattern moves on.
core.h: Wave speed and the wave equation
core.p: The **wave speed** is how fast the wave pattern (and so the energy) moves through the medium. The wave equation links speed to frequency and wavelength: **wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)**, written **v = f × λ**. It works because in one second f waves pass a point, and each wave is λ long, so the pattern advances f × λ metres every second. This equation applies to **all waves**: sound, water, light and the whole electromagnetic spectrum.

bullets: Speed of **sound in air** is about **330 m/s**; sound travels faster in liquids and faster still in solids because particles are closer together.
Speed of **all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum** is about **3.0 × 10^8 m/s** (in air almost the same).
Speed of **water waves** depends on the depth of the water: waves travel more slowly in shallow water.
Changing the **amplitude** does not change the speed.
Changing the **frequency** of the source changes the wavelength, not the speed (in the same medium).
When a wave enters a different medium: **frequency unchanged**, speed changes, so **wavelength changes in the same proportion**.
Use v = f λ with the right speed for the medium: sound 330 m/s in air, light 3 × 10^8 m/s.
core.h: What determines the speed of a wave?
core.p: The speed of a wave depends on the **medium** it travels through (and for some waves on properties like depth or temperature), not on its amplitude. The **frequency** is fixed by the source. So when a wave changes medium its speed changes but its **frequency stays the same**, which means the **wavelength must change** (since v = f λ). This is the key idea behind refraction in a later topic.

bullets: Step 1: list what you are given and what you need (e.g. v = 330 m/s, f = 440 Hz, find λ).
Step 2: write the equation in the form for the unknown, e.g. λ = v ÷ f.
Step 3: convert units (km to m, cm to m, kHz to Hz, MHz to Hz, minutes to seconds).
Step 4: substitute and calculate: 330 ÷ 440 = 0.75.
Step 5: write the answer with the unit: 0.75 m.
Step 6: check it is sensible (a 440 Hz sound in air has a wavelength under 1 m).
Standard form: enter 3.0 × 10^8 as 3.0 EXP 8 or ×10^x on your calculator, not 3.0 × 108.
core.p: Wave calculation questions are usually 2 or 3 marks and are very predictable. The method is the same each time: **write the equation, rearrange if needed, convert units to standard (m, Hz, m/s, s), substitute, calculate, and give the unit**. Mark schemes give a mark for the equation or rearrangement, a mark for substitution and a mark for the answer with unit, so showing each step protects marks even if the final arithmetic is wrong.

bullets: Distance axis: wavelength = distance between two successive crests.
Time axis: period = time between two successive crests; f = 1 ÷ T.
Amplitude is the height from the **axis** (the rest position) to the crest, on either graph.
Read the scale carefully: check the units and the size of each division (and whether the axis is in ms or cm).
If a graph shows 2.5 waves over 0.05 s, the period is 0.05 ÷ 2.5 = 0.02 s, and f = 50 Hz.
The two graphs can look identical; only the **axis label** tells you which quantity you read.
To find the wave speed from graphs you need both wavelength (distance graph) and frequency (time graph): v = f λ.
core.h: Reading wavelength, amplitude, period and frequency from graphs
core.p: Two types of graph are used and you must not mix them up. A **displacement-distance graph** is a snapshot of the whole wave at one instant, so its horizontal axis is **distance** and you can read the **wavelength** and **amplitude**. A **displacement-time graph** follows **one point** as the wave passes, so its horizontal axis is **time** and you can read the **period** and amplitude, then calculate **frequency = 1 ÷ period**.

bullets: Sound in air: about **330 m/s** (at normal temperatures).
Light and all EM waves in a vacuum: about **3.0 × 10^8 m/s**.
Human hearing range: about **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz** (20 kHz). Ultrasound is above 20 000 Hz.
Mains frequency in the UK: 50 Hz (period 0.02 s).
Visible light frequency: about 4 × 10^14 Hz to 8 × 10^14 Hz.
Radio waves have long wavelengths and low frequencies; gamma rays have very short wavelengths and high frequencies.
core.h: Typical wave speeds and frequencies to know
core.p: You should know a few typical values to check whether an answer is reasonable and to use in calculations when they are not given in the question. These are consistent with the specification where it states that the speed of sound in air is about 330 m/s and that electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.

bullets: Speed = distance ÷ time; in 1 s the wave moves f wavelengths, so v = f × λ.
Alternatively, in one period T the wave travels exactly one wavelength: v = λ ÷ T. Since 1/T = f, this is the same as v = f λ.
This is why **higher frequency means shorter wavelength** for a given speed.
It also explains why the equation holds for sound, water waves and light alike.
Check your units: Hz × m = (1/s) × m = m/s.
You may be asked to show this reasoning in a 'show that' question.
core.h: Worked reasoning: why v = f λ
core.p: It helps to see why the equation is true rather than just memorising it. Imagine standing beside a canal counting waves go past point P. If 4 waves pass every second, then the frequency is 4 Hz. If each wave is 0.5 m long, then after one second the front of the first wave has moved a distance of 4 wavelengths, 4 × 0.5 = 2 m. So the wave speed is 2 m/s. Writing this generally, **distance moved in one second = number of waves per second × length of each wave = f × λ**.

bullets: **Refraction**: moving into a denser material slows a wave; f is constant so λ decreases.
**EM spectrum**: radio waves (long λ, low f) to gamma (short λ, high f), all at 3.0 × 10^8 m/s in a vacuum.
**Sound**: higher frequency means higher pitch; larger amplitude means louder.
**Ultrasound** and **seismic waves** use the same equation with different speeds.
Ratio reasoning: if f doubles and v is unchanged, λ halves.
Combine with distance = speed × time: e.g. echo problems where sound travels to a wall and back (distance travelled = 2 × distance to wall).
Rearranging with standard form and prefixes is a common Higher test: always convert to Hz and m first.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: The wave equation is used in nearly every other Waves topic. In **refraction** a wave changes speed when it crosses a boundary and the wavelength changes but the frequency does not. In the **electromagnetic spectrum**, all waves have the same speed in a vacuum so higher frequency means shorter wavelength. In **sound**, pitch is determined by frequency and loudness by amplitude. Higher tier questions often combine v = f λ with unit conversions, standard form, or a ratio argument.

bullets: **Transverse examples:** electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays), ripples on water, waves on a rope or string, and S-waves in earthquakes.
**Longitudinal examples:** sound waves in air, ultrasound, and P-waves in earthquakes; a slinky pushed in and out along its length.
**Compression:** a region where the particles are **closer together** than normal (higher pressure for sound).
**Rarefaction:** a region where the particles are **further apart** than normal (lower pressure for sound).
**Wavelength of a longitudinal wave:** the distance from the centre of one compression to the centre of the next compression.
Transverse waves can travel through a vacuum only if they are electromagnetic; sound (longitudinal) **needs a medium** and cannot travel through a vacuum.
Exam wording: 'the oscillations are **perpendicular** to the direction of energy transfer' (transverse) and '**parallel** to' (longitudinal).
core.p: Waves can be described by comparing the direction the particles of the medium vibrate with the direction the wave travels. In a **transverse wave** the oscillations are at **right angles (perpendicular)** to the direction of energy transfer, as on a rope shaken up and down, so crests and troughs appear. In a **longitudinal wave** the oscillations are **parallel** to the direction of energy transfer, so the medium is squashed into **compressions** and stretched into **rarefactions**. Both kinds are described by the same four quantities and the same wave equation, so you must be able to say which type a named wave is.

bullets: Evidence: a floating cork or duck on a water wave moves up and down but does not travel with the wave.
Sound from a speaker reaches you because air particles vibrate to and fro, not because air flows from the speaker to your ear.
Information (a radio or phone signal, speech) is carried by the wave, but nothing material is moved from sender to receiver.
Energy is transferred in the direction the wave travels; the larger the amplitude, the more energy per second is carried.
Particle speed (continually changing) is **not** the same as wave speed (steady in a given medium).
Say 'energy is transferred' in exam answers, never 'the particles are carried along'.
core.p: The AQA specification states that waves transfer **energy** and **information** from one place to another, but the **matter of the medium does not travel with the wave**. Each particle only vibrates about a fixed position, passing the energy on to its neighbour. You can see this when a cork floating on water bobs up and down on the spot while the ripples carry on past it. A wave is therefore a moving pattern of disturbance, and the wave speed is the speed of that pattern, not the speed of the particles.

bullets: **Reflected:** a wave bounces back, e.g. an echo of sound or light from a mirror.
**Absorbed:** wave energy is passed to the material, e.g. a black surface absorbs light and gets warmer; a soft fabric absorbs sound.
**Transmitted:** the wave continues through, e.g. light through glass or radio waves through a wall.
The proportions depend on the **wavelength** of the wave and the **material**: glass transmits visible light but absorbs much ultraviolet.
When a transmitted wave changes medium its **frequency stays the same** but its speed and wavelength change (v = f λ).
Ripple-tank barriers are used to show reflection: a straight wave bounces off a flat barrier and keeps the same wavelength.
core.p: When a wave meets a boundary between two different materials it can be **reflected**, **absorbed** or **transmitted**, and often all three happen in different proportions. In **reflection** the wave bounces back off the surface. In **absorption** the wave energy is transferred to the material, which usually warms up. In **transmission** the wave carries on through the material, and it may change speed and direction, which is refraction. What happens depends on the wavelength of the wave and the properties of the material, so a given material may absorb one type of wave and transmit another.

bullets: **Wavelength:** measure the distance across **several** wavelengths on the screen with a ruler (e.g. 5 wavelengths = 10.0 cm) and divide, which reduces the percentage uncertainty.
**Frequency:** read it from the signal generator or motor setting, or count the number of waves passing a mark in a timed interval and divide by the time.
**Speed:** calculate v = f × λ, converting cm to m first (2.0 cm = 0.020 m); with f = 8.0 Hz, v = 0.16 m/s.
**Control variables:** keep the water depth the same, because depth changes the wave speed; keep the dipper height fixed.

**Waves in a solid:** a signal generator drives a vibration generator attached to a string or spring; adjust f until a clear stable pattern forms, measure the wavelength with a ruler over several loops (one loop is half a wavelength), then use v = f λ.
**Risks:** water on the floor or near electrical equipment (mop spills, keep sockets away from water); a hot lamp; do not look directly into a bright strobe, especially if you are photosensitive.
Use a **fiducial marker** such as a ruler placed in the image when filming so the scale is accurate.
core.h: Required practical: measuring waves in a ripple tank and in a solid
core.p: The specification requires you to make observations to identify suitable apparatus to measure the **frequency, wavelength and speed** of waves in a **ripple tank** and waves in a **solid**, and to take appropriate measurements. In a ripple tank a motor-driven dipper makes straight ripples; a lamp above shines light through the water so that a pattern of bright and dark lines forms on white paper or a screen beneath, and a **strobe** (or a photo or video with a ruler in view) freezes the pattern so the wavelength can be measured. Frequency comes from the setting of the motor or signal generator, or by counting waves passing a point in a measured time, and the speed is then calculated from **v = f λ**.

bullets: **Echo method:** stand a measured distance d from a wall, clap, time the echo; speed = 2d ÷ t.
Example: d = 85 m and t = 0.52 s gives speed = (2 × 85) ÷ 0.52 = 327 m/s.
**Two microphones:** distance between microphones divided by the time delay shown on the timer.
Repeat several times and take a **mean** to reduce the effect of random error in human reaction time.
Use a long distance so the timing error is a small fraction of the total time.
Once you know the speed, rearrange v = f λ to find the wavelength of a sound of known frequency, e.g. 440 Hz gives 0.75 m.
core.h: Measuring the speed of sound: two ways
core.p: The specification gives the speed of sound in air as about **330 m/s**, and you should be able to describe how it can be measured and then use v = f λ. In the **echo method** a sound is made a measured distance from a flat wall, and the time for the sound to travel to the wall and back is measured; the speed is the total distance divided by the time. In the **two-microphone method** a sound reaches two microphones a known distance apart connected to a timer, and the speed is the distance between them divided by the time difference. Both methods use **speed = distance ÷ time** for a wave, which is why the answer should be close to 330 m/s.

exam: Recall questions (1 mark): 'State the equation linking wave speed, frequency and wavelength' - wave speed = frequency × wavelength.
Calculation questions (2-3 marks): 1 mark for correct rearrangement/equation, 1 for substitution (with converted units), 1 for the answer with the unit.
Always convert to base units: Hz not kHz or MHz; m not cm, mm or km.
If two significant figures are given in the data, give your answer to two or three significant figures unless told otherwise.

'Describe the wavelength / amplitude' (1 mark each) must use the board definitions: 'distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave' and 'maximum displacement from the undisturbed position'.
Graph questions: say what you read from the graph (e.g. 'crest to crest = 0.02 s'), then calculate f = 1 ÷ T.
'Explain' questions about waves entering a new medium: state frequency unchanged, wave speed changes, so wavelength changes (v = fλ).
Show-that questions: write the answer to more significant figures than the one given, then show the rounded value.
Check the answer is sensible: sound wavelengths in air are metres or less, light wavelengths are about 10^-7 m.
Marks for units are often lost: write 'm/s', 'Hz', 'm' and 's' every time.
**Transverse or longitudinal (2 marks):** say which, then link to the direction of the oscillations: 'perpendicular to' or 'parallel to the direction of energy transfer'.

**Required practical (6 marks):** name the measuring tools (ruler, stopwatch or strobe), say measure several wavelengths and divide, state f from the generator, then calculate v = fλ and give the control variable (depth).

mistakes.w: Wavelength is measured from a crest to a trough.

mistakes.w: Using kHz, MHz, cm or km directly in v = f λ.

mistakes.r: Give the unit: m/s for speed, Hz for frequency, m for wavelength, s for period.
mistakes.w: Writing the answer without a unit, or with the wrong unit.

mistakes.w: A bigger amplitude makes the wave travel faster.

summary: You must be able to describe a wave using its amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period, and to use the equations wave speed = frequency × wavelength (v = f λ) and period = 1 ÷ frequency (T = 1/f), including rearranging them and handling units. It matters because this one equation links every wave in the course, from sound and water waves to the whole electromagnetic spectrum. The AQA 4.6.1.2 wording also covers transverse and longitudinal waves, energy (not matter) being transferred, reflection, absorption and transmission, and the required practical on waves in a ripple tank and in a solid.

The material a wave travels through.
Two quantities where one doubles as the other halves; for a constant wave speed, wavelength and frequency.

worked.q: A sound wave in air has a frequency of 440 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. Calculate the wavelength. [3 marks]
steps: Equation: wave speed = frequency × wavelength, so λ = v ÷ f.

worked.q: 12 water waves pass a floating buoy in 6.0 seconds. The distance between successive crests is 0.25 m. Calculate (a) the frequency and (b) the wave speed. [4 marks]
steps: (a) f = number of waves ÷ time = 12 ÷ 6.0 = 2.0 Hz.
